profile.summary: Ezekiel is a prophetic book shaped by the crisis of Babylonian exile and the fall of Jerusalem. He begins with disconcerting visions of God's moving glory, calls the prophet to speak to a hard people of heart, and then firmly announces that judgment on Judah and Jerusalem is inevitable. After the destruction of the city, the book turns to hope: God has not forsaken his people, but promises to restore him, purify him, gather the scattered, renew his relationship with them, and return to dwell among them. The whole bow goes from judgment to restoration, showing that the holiness of God and his faithfulness to the covenant go together. For evangelical readers, Ezekiel highlights God's sovereignty in history, the gravity of sin, the need for repentance and the promise of new life that finds its full fulfillment in Christ.
profile.setting: Ezekiel was written in the context of the exile of Judah in Babylon, between 605 and 538 B.C., with the first visions of the prophet dating from 593 BC, when he was about thirty years old. The historical background includes the Babylonian ascent, the taking of exiles in 605 and 597 BC, the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the period in which the people remained away from the land. The authorship is traditionally attributed to the prophet himself, and the introduction considers this claim plausible; the final composition was probably completed shortly after the last recorded message, still within the period of Ezekiel's ministry. Literarily, the book combines visions, symbolic acts, oracles, poems and final descriptions of temple and earth, with strong thematic unity centered on the glory of God, judgment and restoration.

structure.label: Called and Sending the Prophet
structure.description: Inaugural view of God's glory, prophetic commission and responsibility to act as a sentinel before a resilient people.

structure.label: Signs of the siege and denunciation of Jerusalem's guilt
structure.description: Symbolic act and scenes that announce the siege, expose the corruption of the city and show the withdrawal of the glory of the Lord from the sanctuary.

structure.label: Judgement about Judah and Jerusalem
structure.description: Oracles and images reaffirm the inevitability of destruction, culminating in the confirmation of the trial against the city.

structure.label: Oracles against the nations
structure.description: Messages against neighboring peoples who rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem and opposed the purposes of God.

structure.label: New phase of hope and restoration
structure.description: After the news of the fall, the prophet goes back to speak as a sentinel and announces a new pastor, renewal of the people, reunification and the final defeat of the enemies.

structure.label: Final view of the temple and the earth
structure.description: An architectural, ritual and territorial description of a future in which God dwells again in the midst of his people, with life flowing from the temple.

themes: The holiness of God and the need for purification of his people
Judgment as a real response to persistent sin and false religious security
The sovereign restoration of God after the catastrophe
God's presence among his people as the centre of hope
Spiritual renewal, new implicit covenant and life that overcomes death
readingKeys: Notice the progression of the book: vision, denunciation, judgment, hope and consummation; Ezekiel is not a random collection, but a clear theological movement.
Read the images carefully: many passages are symbolic and work to reveal truths about God, sin and restoration, not just to describe literal events in a simple way.
Note the contrast between the withdrawal and the return of God's glory: this thread unites the crisis of exile to the final hope of divine habitation among the people.
profile.cautions: Ezekiel uses highly figurative language, strange visions and symbolic acts; therefore, reading requires care not to turn every image into speculation. The book speaks with severity about sin, idolatry, and judgment, but its goal is not to despair the reader, but to lead him to reverence, repentance and hope in God's faithfulness. Although tradition attributes the book to Ezekiel himself and the introduction considers this authorship probable, the exact date of the final essay is presented with caution.

dossier.narratedEra: The book situates its prophetic narrative at the time of Judah's Babylonian exile, especially between the deportation of 597 BC and the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, with Ezekiel's first vision in 593 BC in Babylon. The narrated horizon includes the period in which Judah was vasalized, the rebellion of Zedekiah, the siege and destruction of Jerusalem, and then the post-586 hope phase, culminating in the final vision of restoration, temple and land in Ezekiel 40-48.
dossier.compositionEra: Tyndale's source of introduction understands that Ezekiel probably wrote during the period when the views and messages were given, i.e., approximately 593-571 BC, with the final composition possibly shortly after the last message. Matthew Henry also locates him at the beginning of exile, while the exiles were still in Babylon. The authorship is traditionally attributed to the prophet himself in Ez 1:3, and Tyndale's source says that there is little reason to doubt this claim.

politics.title: Babylonian exile as a central political scene
politics.detail: Ezekiel prophesies among the deportees of Judah in Babylon under Babylonian imperial domination. The introduction itself describes Judah as living under subjugation from 597 BC, and Babylon as the power that controls the destiny of the kingdom.
politics.readingImpact: Reading the book as prophecy in imperial context helps to understand why the glory of the Lord appears far from Jerusalem: God remains sovereign even outside the earth and the temple.

politics.title: Jehoakim, Jehoakim/Jeconias and the first deportation
politics.detail: The introduction places the political crisis in 605 BC, when Babylon defeats the last remnant of Assyrian resistance and then makes raids on Judah, taking hostages of the elite, including Daniel and his companions. Then Jehoshakikim rebels in 601 BC and dies in the subsequent siege; his son Jehoiakim is taken into exile in 597 BC.
politics.readingImpact: The background of rebellion and deportation explains why the book's messages alternate between judgment and preservation of a remnant: Judah's political infidelity is read as part of the greater spiritual guilt.

politics.title: Zedekiah as vassal and the final rupture
politics.detail: Babylon puts Zedekiah, the uncle of Jehoiakim/Jeoniah, on the throne of Judah as a vassal king. When he rebels, the Babylonians surround Jerusalem in January 588 BC and the city falls in August 586 BC; the temple is destroyed and Zedekiah is blinded and brought to Babylon.
politics.readingImpact: This framework helps to read the oracles of condemnation in response to a real political conflict, but prophetically interpreted as divine judgment on the city, temple and leadership.

politics.title: Nebucadnezar as agent of the divine decree
politics.detail: The source points out that God ruled even Nebucadnezar's attempts to consult his gods for divination, and that the Babylonian king was only an agent of the divine decision against Jerusalem. In Ez 24, the final attack is presented as the inevitable fulfillment of the announced judgment.
politics.readingImpact: This prevents a reading in which Babylon would be the ultimate power; the book wants the reader to see the empire as an instrument subordinate to the government of YHWH.

politics.title: The neighbouring nations and the dispute for the fall of Jerusalem
politics.detail: In Ez 2532, according to the introduction, the peoples around Judah are judged to have helped the Babylonians and to rejoice in the fall of Jerusalem. Reading associates this with the Abrahamic promise of Gn 12:3.
politics.readingImpact: Prophecies against nations broaden political reading: the fall of Jerusalem is not a definitive victory of the neighbors, but a moment that also puts them under judgment.

customs.title: Priestly service at the age of 30
customs.detail: In Ez 1:1, Tyndale observes that priests began to minister in the temple of Jerusalem at the age of thirty. Ezekiel is a priest of birth, but he is in exile and therefore prevented from exercising the cult in the usual way.
customs.readingImpact: The priestly detail makes the initial vision more poignant: the prophet sees the glory of God away from the temple, a sign that access to the Lord does not depend solely on the culture geography of Jerusalem.

customs.title: Impurity, mourning and priestly restrictions
customs.detail: When Ezekiel's wife dies, he cannot mourn publicly. The note explains that practices such as tearing up the garments and dismantling would become one ritually unclean, and priests could not be contaminated by the dead outside of the closest relatives.
customs.readingImpact: The prophet's personal pain becomes a public sign: the reader realizes that judgment on Jerusalem is so severe that even normal forms of mourning will be suspended.

customs.title: Sacrifice, table and image of the meltinger
customs.detail: In Ez 24:1-14, the cooking pot evokes expectations of food and communion, but here it becomes a figure of Jerusalem. The note also uses sacrificial language: the "best pieces" and the act of "finishing the hand" reminds the imposition of the hand on the offer.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands that the city, which should be a place of worship and communion, became something to be consumed in judgment; the image reverses the table of grace on the scene of destruction.

customs.title: Blood exposed and urban guilt
customs.detail: The note states that Jerusalem was filled with shed blood and did not cover it with land, contrary to the demand of Lv 17:13. This is described as double guilt, aggravated by the exposure of innocent blood.
customs.readingImpact: Impurity is not only moral, but also cultual and social; the text is now read as a denunciation of public violence that corrupts the city in its entirety.

customs.title: Culture of exile and identity preservation
customs.detail: The introduction says that the Babylonians normally resettled people by ethnic groups and allowed them to maintain their identity, unlike the Assyrian policy of dispersion. He also mentions that the Quebar canal was located in the Nipur region of southeastern Babylon.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to understand why the exiled people can remain as a recognizable community and listen to prophets in exile, rather than simply disappear as a group.

language.title: Language of theophany and descriptive difficulty
language.detail: In Ez 1:4-28, Tyndale observes the frequent use of expressions such as "parecia," "algo" as "and "similar," because Ezekiel struggles to describe what he sees. The scene is presented as God's physical manifestation in judgment.
language.readingImpact: The hesitant language does not weaken the vision; on the contrary, it communicates the transcendence of the Lord and prepares the reader for a book in which divine glory exceeds the common language.

language.title: Divine car of war
language.detail: The vision of the wind/storm, of the living beings and the wheels is read as a chariot of divine warfare. The wheels allow movement in any direction, symbolizing God's freedom to judge; the eyes on the wheels increase terror and prevent any concealment.
language.readingImpact: The literary context transforms divine glory into a proclamation of judicial persecution: God comes, not as immediate refuge, but as a warrior against rebellious Jerusalem.

language.title: Number four and fullness created
language.detail: The four living beings are linked to number four as a symbol of completeness; their faces (lion, ox, eagle, and man) represent the apex of the animal world and of creation. Tyndale also notes similarities with mesopotamian guardians of palaces.
language.readingImpact: The vision gains a cosmic dimension: it deals not only with Jerusalem, but of God's rule over all created order and on the imperial symbols of the Babylonian world.

language.title: Image of the throne and man on it
language.detail: In Ez 1:26-27, the figure like a man on the throne communicates the shining glory of the Lord, associated with the tabernacle and the temple. The note says that the vision anticipates the coming of God in human form in Jesus Christ.
language.readingImpact: The image is not only apocalyptic; it guides Christian reading and emphasizes that God's presence can be recognized in a form that exceeds Jerusalem's cult expectations.

language.title: Rainbow as a mixture of judgment and mercy
language.detail: The rainbow at Ez 1:28 is interpreted as a sign of hope with the cloud of judgment, referring to the post-luviation covenant of Gn 9:12-17. The note highlights that the destruction of Jerusalem would not be the final word.
language.readingImpact: The reader is trained to see hope embedded in the sentence: even when glory comes in storm, judgment is tempered by promise of remnant.

language.title: Access vocabulary, center and shore on restored land
language.detail: In Ez 48, the description in east-west bands and the emphasis on the sacrum axis organize the land around the temple. There is a clear distinction between holy center and less privileged margins; the final name of the city is "The Lord."
language.readingImpact: Geographical language shapes theological reading: the restored space is not neutral, but hierarchical by holiness and divine presence.

timeline.title: 612-605 BC: Babylonian ascent on the ancient Assyrian world
timeline.detail: The introduction places the capture of Nineveh in 612 BC and the decisive victory of Carquemis in 605 BC, when Babylonian domination over the ancient Assyrian scenario is completed. That same year, Babylon invades Judah and takes hostages of the elite.
timeline.readingImpact: The beginning of the book is part of the geopolitical turn of the ancient Near East, which explains the sense of historical collapse in which Ezekiel prophesies.

timeline.title: 597 BC: deportation of Jehoiakim and Ezekiel
timeline.detail: Jehoiakim surrenders and is taken to Babylon in 597 BC; at the same time Ezekiel and other notable ones are deported, while temple treasures are plundered.
timeline.readingImpact: This landmark sets the starting point of the prophet among the exiles and clarifies why the book insists on God's presence outside Jerusalem.

timeline.title: 593 BC: first vision of Ezekiel
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the first visions took place in Babylon in 593 BC, when Ezekiel was thirty years old. Ez 1:1-2 is also read as dating the first divine word in the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiakim/Jeconias.
timeline.readingImpact: The date reinforces the identity of the book as a message of a prophet-priest in exile, before the final fall of Jerusalem.

timeline.title: 588-586 BC: siege, breach, and destruction of Jerusalem
timeline.detail: The introduction describes the siege of January 588 BC and the destruction of August 586 BC. Tyndale associates Ez 24 with the moment the attack has already begun and Ezekiel announces the certainty of the fall; 24:25-27 also anticipates the day when a survivor will confirm ruin.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology helps to read the passage of the threat discourse to the historical confirmation of judgment, and then to the opening of a new cycle of hope.

timeline.title: 33:21 as a pastoral and historical turning point
timeline.detail: The introduction highlights that in Ez 33:21 the exiles finally receive news of the destruction of Jerusalem. From there, the message shifts from condemnation to consolation and restoration.
timeline.readingImpact: This moment is the narrative key of the book: the lament for loss gives way to the vision of renewal, new pastor, new covenant and new land.

timeline.title: Book end: vision of the temple and restored land
timeline.detail: The introduction and Tyndale 48 treat Ez 40-48 as the consummation of hope: final temple, reorientated land, river of life and city whose name is The Lord is There. Matthew Henry also sums up the second half as part of Israel's restoration and city and temple re-stabilization.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology of the book culminates in a post-judgment vision: history does not end in the destruction of 586 BC, but in the renewal of God's presence among the people.

investigation: Tyndale's source attributes the book to Ezekiel himself based on Ez 1:3 and states that there is little reason to doubt this traditional authorship; Matthew Henry also treats Ezekiel as the penman of prophecy.

As for the composition, Tyndale proposes that the book was written during the period of visions and messages (approx. 593-571 BC), with final writing right after the last message; this is presented as inference of the book structure.

There is a slight difference in emphasis between the sources: Tyndale organizes the book for before/after 586 BC, while Matthew Henry accentuates the progression of judgment to the consolation and notes that Ezekiel and Daniel prophesy at different times of exile.

Messianic Christian reading is explicitly present in Tyndale (e.g. connections with Christ in Ez 1, 34, 36-37 and 47), but this is a devotional interpretive layer, not a historical reconstruction of the sixth century BC.
The historical details available are selective: the sources give striking dates of Jerusalem's exile and fall, but do not offer complete chronology of the entire period of prophetic activity.

The notes highlight strong literary and cultual symbolism; however, several relations between images and meanings are interpretations of the secondary source itself, not directly explained by the biblical text.
Matthew Henry mentions ancient traditions about Ezekiel's death, but the source itself presents them as tradition, not as a safe given; therefore they were not used as a main historical fact.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, without resorting to external knowledge. Therefore, some areas are inevitably selective: there is much coverage of the prologue (Ez 1-3), the judgment on Jerusalem (especially Ez 24) and the final vision (Ez 48), but little specific information about other chapters. The dates are kept only when the sources provide them; when there is editorial inference, it was marked as interpretation. The policy section favors rulers and disputes explicitly mentioned; that of customs focuses on worship, mourning, sacrifice and practices of exile; that of language brings together images and resources that the notes actually discuss. There were no gaps with general historical reconstructions or with etymologies not present in the sources.
